note: Billionaire Life prototype. Every date and number below appears in at least one cited source. Situations and outcomes are summarized in our own words and simplified. Alternatives are generic choices for the game, not claims about what he considered.

person.name: Mark Zuckerberg
person.role: Founder, Chairman and CEO of Meta Platforms
person.bio: Founded the company now called Meta in 2004 and has been its CEO ever since; chairman of its board since 2012. He attended Harvard University, where he studied computer science.

school.name: The Hacker Way
school.tagline: Move fast, connect everyone, keep founder control and fund long bets on the next platform.

principles.name: Move fast, stay lean
principles.summary: His 2012 IPO letter described a culture of shipping small improvements quickly and learning from them, with the saying "Move fast and break things." In 2023 he argued that every extra management layer slows decisions, so a flatter, leaner company moves faster.

sources.title: Facebook registration statement (Form S-1), including Letter from Mark Zuckerberg
Update on Meta's Year of Efficiency

principles.name: Own the networks people use
principles.summary: He framed the company's mission as making the world more open and connected. Facebook bought popular apps with big user bases, Instagram and then WhatsApp, and said both would keep growing independently under their own brands.

sources.title: Facebook registration statement (Form S-1), including Letter from Mark Zuckerberg
Facebook to Acquire Instagram
Facebook to Acquire WhatsApp

principles.name: Keep founder control
principles.summary: Facebook went public with two share classes: Class B shares carry ten votes each, Class A shares one. That structure lets him control shareholder votes, and he has kept majority voting control even after pledging substantially all of his shares to giving.

sources.title: Facebook registration statement (Form S-1), including Letter from Mark Zuckerberg
Facebook current report (Form 8-K), December 1, 2015
Meta Platforms 2026 proxy statement

principles.name: Make money to build
principles.summary: His IPO letter said: "we don't build services to make money; we make money to build better services." In 2021 he cited that line to explain very large, long-term investments in what he saw as the next platform, the metaverse.

sources.title: Facebook registration statement (Form S-1), including Letter from Mark Zuckerberg
Founder's Letter, 2021

decisions.title: Buy the hot photo app?
decisions.situation: Your social network is eight years old and sharing photos is one of the main reasons people use it. A small San Francisco startup, Instagram, has a mobile photo-sharing app that millions of people love.

options.label: Build your own mobile photo features instead
Buy Instagram for about $1 billion and let it run on its own
Take a small stake and see how it grows

decisions.actual: On April 9, 2012 Facebook agreed to buy Instagram for about $1 billion in cash and Facebook shares. He promised to keep growing Instagram as its own app rather than fold it into Facebook, and called it the first time the company had bought a product with so many users.
decisions.outcome: In December 2020 the FTC sued, arguing the Instagram and WhatsApp deals were used to protect a monopoly. After a trial in 2025, the court ruled in Meta's favor on November 18, 2025; the FTC filed an appeal on January 20, 2026 (as of Meta's report for the quarter ended June 30, 2026).

sources.title: Facebook to Acquire Instagram
FTC Sues Facebook for Illegal Monopolization
Meta quarterly report (Form 10-Q), quarter ended June 30, 2026

lesson.takeaway: The idea: buy a popular network with many users, and keep what its users love instead of folding everything into your own app.
lesson.watchOut: He said then that Facebook did not plan many more deals like it, yet it bought WhatsApp two years later; the FTC's 2020 lawsuit cited both deals, the court ruled for Meta in November 2025, and the FTC has appealed.

decisions.title: Pay up for a messaging app?
decisions.situation: WhatsApp, a messaging app based in Mountain View, has over 450 million monthly users and is adding more than 1 million new registered users a day. It makes very little money.

options.label: Push your own Messenger app harder instead
Offer WhatsApp a partnership, not a purchase
Buy WhatsApp for about $16 billion plus $3 billion in staff stock

decisions.actual: On February 19, 2014 Facebook agreed to buy WhatsApp for about $16 billion ($4 billion cash and about $12 billion in shares), plus $3 billion in restricted stock for its founders and staff. WhatsApp kept its brand and co-founder Jan Koum joined Facebook's board. The deal closed in October 2014.
decisions.outcome: The FTC later counted the deal at $19 billion and challenged it together with Instagram; the court ruled for Meta in November 2025 and the FTC has appealed. Meta's apps reached 3.58 billion daily active people on average in December 2025.

sources.title: Facebook to Acquire WhatsApp
Facebook annual report (Form 10-K), 2014
FTC Sues Facebook for Illegal Monopolization
Meta annual report (Form 10-K), 2025

lesson.takeaway: Paying for users before revenue is a bet that a huge, fast-growing network can become valuable later.
lesson.watchOut: Facebook's 2014 annual report said it made money from WhatsApp in only a very limited way, and the deal became part of the FTC's case; the court ruled for Meta in November 2025 and the FTC has appealed.

decisions.title: What to do with the fortune?
decisions.situation: You own roughly 4 million Class A and 419 million Class B Facebook shares, worth about $45 billion. You want to fund work on things like disease and education, but you also want to keep control of the company.

options.label: Give a slice each year to a classic charity foundation
Pledge 99% of your shares to a new organization you control
Hold the shares and decide on giving later in life

decisions.actual: On December 1, 2015 he and Priscilla Chan said they would give 99% of their Facebook shares, then worth about $45 billion, over their lifetimes through the new Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, an LLC he controls. Facebook's filing said he planned to sell or give no more than $1 billion of stock a year for the next three years and keep majority voting control.
decisions.outcome: On November 6, 2025 the couple said their Biohub science group would go 'all in' on combining AI with biology to help cure or prevent disease. He still held 60.8% of Meta's voting power as of April 1, 2026, much of it through Chan Zuckerberg holding companies.

sources.title: Facebook current report (Form 8-K), December 1, 2015
Mark Zuckerberg Says He Plans to Give Away 99 Percent of His Facebook Shares
Biohub launches first large-scale scientific initiative combining frontier AI with frontier biology
Meta Platforms 2026 proxy statement

lesson.takeaway: Giving through an LLC he controls let him pledge most of his shares while keeping majority voting control of the company.
lesson.watchOut: Facebook's IPO filing warned that this concentrated control limits other shareholders' ability to influence company decisions.

sources.title: Facebook registration statement (Form S-1), including Letter from Mark Zuckerberg

decisions.title: Rename the company after the future?
decisions.situation: Your company is named after its first app, but it now runs several apps plus Quest virtual-reality headsets. You believe the next big platform will be an immersive, shared online world: the metaverse.

options.label: Keep the Facebook name and treat VR as a side project
Rename the company Meta and make the metaverse its focus
Spin VR off into a separate company

decisions.actual: On October 28, 2021, at the Connect conference, he introduced Meta as the new company brand, with a focus on bringing the metaverse to life. The company also announced a $150 million investment in immersive learning.
decisions.outcome: The name stuck, but the bet is costly: the Reality Labs unit lost $19.19 billion in 2025, up from $17.73 billion in 2024. Meta now puts much of its spending into AI: in its report for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 it expected $130 billion to $145 billion of capital spending in 2026 to support its AI efforts and core business, up from $115 billion to $135 billion in its annual report.

sources.title: Introducing Meta: A Social Technology Company
Meta annual report (Form 10-K), 2025
Meta quarterly report (Form 10-Q), quarter ended June 30, 2026

lesson.takeaway: A long-term platform bet means spending heavily for years on something that may not pay off soon; he said the business was built to support investments like this.
lesson.watchOut: The bet is costly: Reality Labs had a $19.19 billion operating loss in 2025, and Meta now says its planned 2026 capital spending of $130 billion to $145 billion is to support its AI efforts and core business.

sources.title: Founder's Letter, 2021

decisions.title: Cut again, or hold steady?
decisions.situation: In November 2022 you cut about 13% of staff, more than 11,000 people. Business is still difficult and you have named 2023 the 'Year of Efficiency'.

options.label: Stop at one round of layoffs and protect morale
Cut about 10,000 more jobs and flatten the company
Freeze hiring only and wait for growth to return

decisions.actual: On March 14, 2023 he told employees Meta would shrink by about 10,000 more people, close about 5,000 open roles it had not filled, flatten management layers and cancel lower-priority projects. Affected employees were told between March and May 2023.
decisions.outcome: Meta's net income rose to $39.10 billion in 2023 from $23.20 billion in 2022, and headcount was 67,317 at the end of 2023, down 22%. On February 1, 2024 Meta announced its first-ever cash dividend.

sources.title: Mark Zuckerberg's Message to Meta Employees
Update on Meta's Year of Efficiency
Meta annual report (Form 10-K), 2023

lesson.takeaway: Fewer management layers and fewer side projects can speed up a big company; he said many things went faster after the first round of cuts.
lesson.watchOut: Cuts have a human cost: he acknowledged the changes caused uncertainty and stress and meant saying goodbye to talented colleagues.

glossary.definition: When one company buys part or all of another company's shares or assets, usually to gain control of it.
When a product becomes more useful as more people use it, like a messaging app that is worth more when all your friends are on it.
Laws meant to protect competition for the benefit of consumers, for example by outlawing illegal monopolization and unlawful mergers.
A setup where a company has two kinds of common stock with different voting power, often so founders keep control while selling shares to the public.
Money a company spends to buy long-term physical assets, such as property and equipment, that it uses in its business.
The profit left after a company subtracts all its costs, interest and taxes from its revenue.
A portion of a company's profit paid out to its shareholders, often on a regular schedule.
